title: U.S. Proposes New Tariffs on 14 Trading Partners — and Mexico Is Not on the List Yet
excerpt: The U.S. trade representative on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, including China and the European Union, over what Washington calls structural excess industrial capacity — with China facing a combined rate of about 45%. No determination has been made on Mexico.
content:
The U.S. trade representative on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, including China and the European Union, over what Washington calls structural excess industrial capacity — a move with direct stakes for Laredo, the nation’s busiest inland port.

The Office of the United States Trade Representative announced affirmative determinations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 in 14 of the 16 “structural excess capacity” investigations it opened on March 11, 2026. The proposed rates run from 15% to 35%, and none of the new tariffs takes effect yet.

China faces the steepest burden. USTR proposed a 20% rate on most Chinese goods, which stacks on top of 25% in Section 301 duties from 2018, for a combined headline rate of about 45% on affected goods. If the U.S.-China trade truce, which expires Jan. 10, 2027, collapses, a fallback rate of up to 40% could apply. About $30 billion in Chinese goods were recommended for relief.

The other proposed rates: the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan face a ceiling of up to 15%; Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand face up to 18%; Singapore faces up to 20%, or 10% if it signs an agreement; India faces up to 25%, or 17% with a deal; and Vietnam faces up to 35%, or 20% with a deal.

Two economies were left out of the determinations for now: Mexico and Norway. USTR said it has not made determinations on either. For Laredo, that matters more than any single rate in the package. The 14 targeted economies supplied $2.07 trillion in U.S. goods imports in 2025 — about 60.5% of America’s $3.41 trillion total — and much of the cargo that moves through the World Trade Bridge is tied to the same global supply chains the new duties would hit. If higher duties on Asian and European goods push more manufacturing and assembly toward Mexico, more of that trade could flow through Laredo; if they slow global trade overall, bridge volumes could feel it the other way. Neither outcome is decided yet.

The action follows the administration’s pivot to Section 301 after federal courts restricted emergency executive tariff authorities. Section 301 actions require public comment periods and investigative findings. Written comments and requests to appear at public hearings are due Jan. 5, 2027, and hearings begin Jan. 25, 2027. USTR said the proposed rates for most partners will generally not stack on top of existing duties, and goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs — including steel, aluminum, vehicles and parts, and semiconductors — would be exempt from the new layer.

Webb Watch 956 will keep watching whether USTR issues a determination on Mexico, and what the final rates mean for cross-border trade through Laredo.

Sources: Reuters — “US proposes new tariffs aimed at factory overcapacity,” Nov. 25, 2026, https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-proposes-new-tariffs-aimed-factory-overcapacity-2026-11-25/; Office of the United States Trade Representative, Section 301 determinations, Nov. 25, 2026; Baker McKenzie, Global Trade & Sanctions Law — “USTR Proposes Section 301 Tariffs on 14 Economies in Structural Excess Capacity Investigations,” Nov. 25, 2026, https://www.globaltradeandsanctionslaw.com/ustr-proposes-section-301-tariffs-on-14-economies-in-structural-excess-capacity-investigations/
